Every source cited in the catalog is one of the references below. Each citation names the specific entry, section or chapter where the fallacy is listed, so a reader can check it. A citation was added only after the page was retrieved and the named entry, section or chapter was found to list that fallacy. An entry with no confirmed source is marked TODO instead of being given a guessed citation.

The definitions and examples in the catalog are written in plain words for this catalog; they are not quotations from these references.

## Notes on the references

- The Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy (IEP) and Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (SEP) are scholarly reference works written by philosophers. SEP Section 1 reviews the core fallacies that most logic textbooks share (following Irving Copi's *Introduction to Logic*), and Section 2 traces the list back to Aristotle, the Port-Royal Logic and Locke.
- Aristotle's *On Sophistical Refutations* is the original list of thirteen fallacies: six that depend on language (chapter 4) and seven that do not (chapters 4 and 5).
- *The Fallacy Files* is a long-running reference site on fallacies maintained by Gary N. Curtis, with one page per fallacy.
- Wikipedia's *List of fallacies* is used as a cross-check of common names; where a fallacy is listed only there, check the citations on that Wikipedia page before relying on it.
- A few statistical errors that are not on the general lists of fallacies are cited to a dedicated reference article: the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry on Simpson's paradox, or individual Wikipedia articles. These are cited by article and section.
